I recently published my project [Postal codes of
Spain](https://dieghernan.github.io/codigospostales/), with estimated postal
areas, an interactive map and GeoPackage downloads. But there is something we
have not looked at yet: how do those address points become polygons? The answer
is... **Voronoi polygons**.

## What is a Voronoi polygon?

Imagine a few shops on a flat map. Which one is closest to your house? Ask that
question for every location and give each shop its own color. The result is a
**Voronoi diagram**, also known as a **Voronoi tessellation**, **Voronoi
decomposition**, **Voronoi partition** or **Dirichlet tessellation**. This
technique divides a plane into regions based on the distance to a given set of
points.

In our example, each shop is a **site**, or generating point. Its **Voronoi
cell**, also called a **Thiessen polygon**, contains the locations at least as
close to that site as to any other. Along a shared edge, two sites are
equally close. Where several cells meet, there may be a tie between more sites.
With ordinary straight-line distance, the edges follow perpendicular bisectors
between sites. Some cells extend indefinitely, so maps usually show them clipped
to a study area.

The name honors Georgy Voronoi, who studied these partitions in the early
twentieth century. The idea has earlier roots, including Dirichlet's
nineteenth-century work (hence the name Dirichlet tessellation). [Pokojski and
Pokojska (2018)](https://doi.org/10.2478/pcr-2018-0009) review the history and
geographical applications.

These partitions are useful for exploring proximity to shops or public services,
assigning areas to weather stations and studying spatial patterns. For example,
Thiessen polygons can supply area weights when estimating rainfall from rain
gauges. The underlying question is always about the chosen distance: the nearest
hospital in a straight line may not be the quickest one to reach.

### A tiny example in **R**

Let's start with five points in an imaginary square, including one at its
center, using just **sf** and **ggplot2**. The coordinates have arbitrary units
and no geographical coordinate reference system.

```{r}
#| label: voronoi-toy-example
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-alt: |
#|   Five labeled sites in a square: A and B below, C and D above, and E at the
#|   center, surrounded by its own bounded Voronoi cell.
#| fig-cap: ""

library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

# Define a common theme for the maps.
background <- "#faf8f2"
ink <- "#203b47"

theme_set(
  theme_void() +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = background, colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = background, colour = NA),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = ink),
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", hjust = 0),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10)
    )
)

sites <- data.frame(
  site = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
  x = c(2, 7, 3, 8, 5),
  y = c(2, 3, 8, 7, 5)
)

toy_points <- st_as_sf(sites, coords = c("x", "y"))

study_area <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(c(xmin = 0, ymin = 0, xmax = 10, ymax = 10)))

toy_cells <- toy_points |>
  st_union() |>
  st_voronoi(envelope = study_area) |>
  st_collection_extract("POLYGON") |>
  st_intersection(study_area)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = toy_cells,
    fill = c("#a8dadc", "#f4c89a", "#c6b8df", "#bfd59b", "#f2b5c4"),
    colour = "white", linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_sf(data = toy_points, colour = "#203b47", size = 3) +
  geom_text(
    data = sites, aes(x, y, label = site),
    nudge_y = 0.5, colour = "#203b47", fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Five points, five Voronoi cells",
    subtitle = "Each location belongs to the closest site"
  )
```

Five points, five cells. The point E at `(5, 5)` has a bounded cell
surrounded by the other four. The outer cells extend beyond the square and are
clipped to its edges. `st_union()` collects the points into one geometry,
`st_voronoi()` builds the diagram and `st_intersection()` clips it to our
square. The colors help us tell the cells apart. We have not assigned any postal
codes yet.

The diagram knows nothing about roads, rivers or administrative boundaries. As
we move to postal points, we will need to make our choices about those
boundaries explicit.

## Before we start: what are we estimating?

The Spanish project uses CartoCiudad address points with their postal codes. It
follows [Goerlich (2022)](https://doi.org/10.12842/WPIVIE_0322), who develops an
idea presented by [Sánchez
(2020)](https://www.nosolosig.com/articulos/asi-hice-el-mapa-de-los-codigos-postales-de-espana-con-sig-y-datos-abiertos).
The [updated online version](https://www.uv.es/goerlich/Ivie/CodPost.html)
describes the method in detail.

For Slovenia, we will use GISCO's postal points, retrieved with **giscoR**.
There is an important difference here: a representative point for a code tells
us much less than thousands of addresses with that code. Detailed addresses help
the partition follow their distribution more closely, although proximity alone
still cannot reproduce postal delivery decisions.

We have not established that Slovenian postal areas should follow municipal
boundaries. Imposing those boundaries is a modeling choice for this exercise,
inspired by the Spanish workflow, rather than a verified property of the
Slovenian postal system.

<i class="fa fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> This post explains the workflow. The
polygons we create are not official postal boundaries, and this exercise does
not validate the GISCO postal data.
{: .alert .alert-warning .p-3 .mx-2 .mb-3}

## Getting the data

First, let's get the municipal boundaries and postal points. We use the 2024
release of both datasets.

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(giscoR)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)

municipalities <- gisco_get_lau(
  year = 2024, country = "SI", epsg = 3035
) |>
  select(GISCO_ID, LAU_NAME) |>
  st_make_valid()

raw_points <- gisco_get_postalcodes(
  year = 2024, country = "SI", epsg = 3035
)
```

We work in **ETRS89 / LAEA Europe (EPSG:3035)**, a projected coordinate system
with coordinates in meters. This makes the 200 m and 50 m margins used later
meaningful. Voronoi uses Euclidean distances in this plane, rather than road
distances. The projection does not preserve every distance exactly either.

Before we start drawing, what have we actually downloaded?

```{r}
#| label: data-summary
postal_points <- raw_points |>
  mutate(POSTCODE = trimws(as.character(POSTCODE))) |>
  filter(!is.na(POSTCODE), POSTCODE != "") |>
  select(POSTCODE)

code_counts <- postal_points |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(POSTCODE, name = "points_per_code")

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Indicator = c(
    "Municipalities", "Downloaded points", "Points with a postal code",
    "Distinct postal codes", "Codes represented by one point"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(municipalities), nrow(raw_points), nrow(postal_points),
    nrow(code_counts), sum(code_counts$points_per_code == 1)
  )
))
```

These counts give us a first look at the file, but they are not a quality check.
They do not establish whether every code is present or whether the coordinates
are correct. With one point per code, we will be drawing areas around
representatives rather than estimating them from individual addresses.

Two points at exactly the same coordinates cannot generate separate Voronoi
cells. We sort by postal code and keep the first point at each location, as in
the original workflow. This is a reproducible tie-breaking rule, not evidence
that the retained code is correct. The counts below show how many records we
remove and how many locations have conflicting codes.

```{r}
#| label: duplicates
postal_points <- postal_points |> arrange(POSTCODE)

conflicts <- postal_points |>
  group_by(geometry) |>
  summarise(codes = n_distinct(POSTCODE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(codes > 1)

duplicates <- duplicated(postal_points$geometry)

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Indicator = c("Duplicate locations removed", "Locations with conflicting codes"),
  Value = c(sum(duplicates), nrow(conflicts))
))

postal_points <- postal_points[!duplicates, ]
```

## Starting with Ljubljana

Let's pick Ljubljana and keep the points inside it. We use `st_within()` so that
a point exactly on a shared boundary is not assigned to both neighboring
municipalities.

```{r}
#| label: ljubljana
#| fig-alt: |
#|   Outline of Ljubljana municipality with six postal point locations marked
#|   inside it.
#| fig-cap: ""

city <- municipalities |> filter(LAU_NAME == "Ljubljana")

city_points <- st_filter(postal_points, city, .predicate = st_within)

base_map <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = city, fill = "#e8e4d8", colour = ink, linewidth = 0.4)

gisco_attr <- gisco_attributions()

base_map +
  geom_sf(data = city_points, colour = "#bd5137", size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Ljubljana: the starting point",
    subtitle = "A municipal boundary and points with postal codes",
    caption = gisco_attr
  )
```

### Building the cells

Each cell contains locations at least as close to its generating point as to
any other point. Cell boundaries occur where distances to two points are equal.
For this first demonstration, we keep all interior points, without the margins used in
the national workflow.

```{r}
#| label: voronoi
#| fig-alt: |
#|   Unclipped Voronoi cells outlined around six postal points, extending beyond
#|   the shaded Ljubljana municipal boundary.
#| fig-cap: ""

cells <- city_points |>
  st_union() |>
  st_voronoi(envelope = st_as_sfc(st_bbox(city))) |>
  st_collection_extract("POLYGON") |>
  st_sf(geometry = _)

base_map +
  geom_sf(data = cells, fill = NA, colour = "#bd5137", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = city_points, colour = ink, size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "An area of proximity for every point",
    subtitle = "Cells still extend beyond the municipal boundary",
    caption = "Own elaboration using data from Eurostat / GISCO, 2024"
  )
```

`st_union()` gathers the points so we build one diagram. One detail to keep in
mind: `envelope` supplies a working extent, but **does not clip** the cells to
the municipality. We need an intersection for that.

### Clipping and recovering postal codes

It would be convenient if cells came out in the same order as the input points,
but we should not rely on that. Instead, we recover each cell's code with a
spatial relationship before clipping. Each cell must contain exactly one
generating point.

```{r}
#| label: clip-cells
#| fig-alt: |
#|   Six colored areas clipped to Ljubljana, labeled 1000, 1210, 1211, 1231, 1260
#|   and 1261, with their generating postal points marked.
#| fig-cap: ""

point_matches <- st_intersects(cells, city_points)

cells$POSTCODE <- city_points$POSTCODE[unlist(point_matches)]

clipped_geometry <- st_intersection(st_geometry(cells), st_geometry(city))

city_cells <- st_sf(
  POSTCODE = cells$POSTCODE[attr(clipped_geometry, "idx")[, 1]],
  geometry = clipped_geometry
)

city_areas <- city_cells |>
  group_by(POSTCODE) |>
  summarise(.groups = "drop") |>
  st_make_valid()

city_colours <- setNames(
  hcl.colors(nrow(city_areas), palette = "Dark 3"),
  sort(city_areas$POSTCODE)
)
city_labels <- st_sf(
  POSTCODE = city_areas$POSTCODE,
  geometry = st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(city_areas))
)

ggplot(city_areas) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = POSTCODE), colour = background, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_sf(
    data = city_points, shape = 21, fill = ink,
    colour = background, size = 2.4
  ) +
  geom_sf_text(
    data = city_labels,
    aes(label = POSTCODE), colour = ink, fontface = "bold", size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = city_colours, guide = "none") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "From points to estimated areas",
    subtitle = "Cells clipped and merged by postal code",
    caption = "Teaching example · Not official postal boundaries"
  )
```

We intersect the geometry columns, then use the intersection's `idx` matrix to
recover each cell's postal code. This keeps the attribute assignment explicit.
Label positions are also calculated from geometries alone.

Grouping by postal code with `summarise()` merges the geometries. With many
addresses sharing a code, their cells would dissolve into one geometry, possibly
with several separate parts.

## From one municipality to the whole country

Ljubljana is done. Now let's repeat the operation for each component of each
municipality. Municipalities can have separate pieces: normalizing to
`MULTIPOLYGON` and then casting to `POLYGON` lets us handle them independently,
without automatically extending a code to a piece with no points.

The municipality ID and name apply to every component, so we mark those
attributes as spatially constant before splitting the geometries.

```{r}
#| label: municipal-components

components <- municipalities |>
  st_set_agr("constant") |>
  st_cast("MULTIPOLYGON") |>
  st_cast("POLYGON") |>
  mutate(component_id = row_number())
```

### Why use an inward margin?

In the Spanish project, we first select addresses within an inward margin of
**200 m**. If none are found, we try **50 m**. This reduces the influence of
points close to a boundary, where small mismatches between layers may affect
their assignment.

There is no universal rule behind these numbers. Goerlich describes a 20 m
margin. The 200 m and 50 m choices come from my implementation. We keep them
here to explain that workflow, although sparse postal points make it easier to
exclude useful information. Comparing other margins would be a useful next step.

```{r}
#| label: select-points

select_points <- function(component, postal_points) {
  for (margin in c(200, 50)) {
    interior <- st_buffer(st_geometry(component), -margin)

    if (all(st_is_empty(interior))) next

    selected_points <- st_filter(postal_points, interior,
      .predicate = st_within
    )

    if (nrow(selected_points) > 0) {
      return(selected_points)
    }
  }

  postal_points[0, ]
}
```

The margin only selects points: the resulting areas cover the **original**
component, not the smaller buffered geometry. If both attempts fail, we leave
the component unassigned. We do not borrow the nearest point from outside the
municipality.

### Three cases, one function

There are three cases to handle. With no points, we keep the component and
assign `NA`. If all selected points share a code, we assign it to the whole
component. We only need Voronoi when several codes are present: no need to split
an area that already has a single assignment.

```{r}
#| label: build-postal-areas

build_areas <- function(component, postal_points) {
  selected_points <- select_points(component, postal_points)

  codes <- unique(selected_points$POSTCODE)

  if (length(codes) <= 1L) {
    component$POSTCODE <- if (length(codes)) codes else NA_character_
    return(component)
  }

  cells <- selected_points |>
    st_union() |>
    st_voronoi(envelope = st_as_sfc(st_bbox(component))) |>
    st_collection_extract("POLYGON") |>
    st_sf(geometry = _)

  point_matches <- st_intersects(cells, selected_points)

  cells$POSTCODE <- selected_points$POSTCODE[unlist(point_matches)]

  clipped_geometry <- st_intersection(
    st_geometry(cells),
    st_geometry(component)
  )

  result <- st_sf(
    POSTCODE = cells$POSTCODE[attr(clipped_geometry, "idx")[, 1]],
    geometry = clipped_geometry
  ) |>
    group_by(POSTCODE) |>
    summarise(.groups = "drop") |>
    st_make_valid()

  result$GISCO_ID <- component$GISCO_ID

  result$LAU_NAME <- component$LAU_NAME

  result$component_id <- component$component_id

  result
}

result <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(components)), function(i) {
  build_areas(components[i, ], postal_points)
}) |>
  bind_rows()
```

### Handling unassigned areas

Can we fill any of the gaps? A component without points may belong to a
municipality whose other components have information. We recover its code only
if the municipality has **one distinct recovered code**. This is an imputation
from the available data, not proof that the municipality really has just one
code.

```{r}
#| label: unassigned

unique_codes <- result |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(POSTCODE)) |>
  distinct(GISCO_ID, POSTCODE) |>
  add_count(GISCO_ID) |>
  filter(n == 1)

unassigned_before <- sum(is.na(result$POSTCODE))

index <- match(result$GISCO_ID, unique_codes$GISCO_ID)

recoverable <- is.na(result$POSTCODE) & !is.na(index)

result$POSTCODE[recoverable] <- unique_codes$POSTCODE[index[recoverable]]
```

Before drawing the final map, let's tidy up the geometries and keep only
surfaces. Repairs can produce collections containing residual lines or points,
which do not belong in an area layer. Dissolving by postal code also removes
municipal boundaries between areas sharing that code.

```{r}
#| label: dissolve-areas
keep_surfaces <- function(x) {
  geometry <- st_make_valid(st_geometry(x))

  geometry <- lapply(geometry, function(part) {
    if (!inherits(part, c("POLYGON", "MULTIPOLYGON", "GEOMETRYCOLLECTION"))) {
      return(st_multipolygon())
    }

    surfaces <- suppressWarnings(st_collection_extract(st_sfc(part), "POLYGON"))

    if (length(surfaces) == 0L || all(st_is_empty(surfaces))) {
      return(st_multipolygon())
    }

    st_cast(st_union(surfaces), "MULTIPOLYGON", warn = FALSE)[[1]]
  })

  st_geometry(x) <- st_sfc(geometry, crs = st_crs(x))

  x[!st_is_empty(x), ]
}

unassigned <- result |>
  filter(is.na(POSTCODE)) |>
  keep_surfaces()

postal_areas <- result |>
  filter(!is.na(POSTCODE)) |>
  group_by(POSTCODE) |>
  summarise(.groups = "drop") |>
  keep_surfaces() |>
  st_cast("MULTIPOLYGON")
```

## The complete map

For the national overview, let's color the areas by the first digit of their
code. This keeps the map readable, without claiming that we have validated a
classification of postal regions. Gray is reserved for unassigned components,
with their own legend entry.

```{r}
#| label: slovenia-postal-codes
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Map of Slovenia showing estimated postal areas for the 20 municipalities
#|   processed in this draft. Colors identify postal prefixes, dark gray marks
#|   unassigned components and light gray shows the remaining municipal background.
#| fig-cap: ""
postal_colours <- c(
  "1" = "#007F7F", "2" = "#E87500", "3" = "#3B6FB6", "4" = "#A64E9A",
  "5" = "#649A32", "6" = "#D9AF00", "8" = "#B94350", "9" = "#6255A4",
  "Unassigned" = "#727A80"
)

postal_groups <- sort(unique(substr(postal_areas$POSTCODE, 1, 1)))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = municipalities, fill = "#d5d2ca", colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(
    data = postal_areas,
    aes(fill = substr(POSTCODE, 1, 1)), colour = background, linewidth = 0.15
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = unassigned, aes(fill = "Unassigned"),
    colour = background, linewidth = 0.15
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = postal_colours, name = "Postal code group",
    breaks = c(postal_groups, "Unassigned"),
    labels = c(paste0(postal_groups, "xxx"), "Unassigned")
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Slovenia, point by point",
    subtitle = "Proximity areas clipped to municipal boundaries",
    caption = paste("Eurostat / GISCO, 2024 · Own elaboration",
      "Dark grey: unassigned areas · Estimated boundaries, not official",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  )
```

## Checking the result

The map is ready, but let's check the geometry before going further. Are the
polygons valid? Do assigned and unassigned areas cover the territory? Are there
any appreciable overlaps? We allow one square meter for numerical differences in
the geometry operations.

```{r}
#| label: geometry-checks
territory <- st_union(st_geometry(municipalities))

coverage <- st_union(c(st_geometry(postal_areas), st_geometry(unassigned)))

difference_m2 <- as.numeric(sum(st_area(st_sym_difference(territory, coverage))))

overlap_m2 <- as.numeric(
  sum(st_area(postal_areas)) + sum(st_area(unassigned)) - sum(st_area(coverage))
)

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Indicator = c(
    "Codes with an estimated area", "Components assigned by municipal recovery",
    "Unassigned records", "Unassigned area (km²)",
    "Coverage difference (m²)", "Overlap (m²)"
  ),
  Value = round(c(
    nrow(postal_areas), sum(recoverable), nrow(unassigned),
    as.numeric(sum(st_area(unassigned))) / 1e6, difference_m2,
    overlap_m2
  ), 4)
))
```

These checks verify the geometry, **not postal accuracy**. We could cover an
entire country with valid polygons and still have a poor approximation of its
delivery areas.

## Back to Spain

We now have the full sequence: points, proximity areas, clipping and merging by
postal code. The same steps work with much more detailed addresses, such as the
CartoCiudad data in my [Spanish postal codes
project](https://dieghernan.github.io/projects/postal-codes-spain).

The input data matters as much as the algorithm. With one representative point
per code, Voronoi mainly maps distances between representatives. With address
points, it can better approximate where each code's addresses are concentrated.
It still knows nothing about delivery routes, physical barriers or official
boundaries.

We have not compared these results with an independent postal source for
Slovenia. Before using them for analysis, we would need to review coverage,
coordinates, the relationship with municipalities and sensitivity to the
margins. For now, we have a working example that shows how the polygons are
built, one step at a time.
